sections.heading: Civil Disobedience & Quit India movements; the INA

blocks.text: The final phase of mass struggle ran through the **Civil Disobedience Movement (1930, begun with the Dandi Salt March), the Quit India Movement (1942, 'Do or Die'), and Subhas Bose's Indian National Army (INA)** — together making British rule untenable and hastening independence.

rows: **Dandi Salt March (12 Mar–6 Apr 1930, 240 mi)**; salt-law breach; **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931); Round Table Conferences; Poona Pact (1932)**.
**Bombay AICC (8 Aug 1942); 'Do or Die'**; leaders jailed; largely spontaneous mass revolt; parallel govts (Tamluk, Satara, **Talcher**).
Founded by **Rash Behari Bose/Mohan Singh**; led by **Subhas Chandra Bose** (1943, Singapore); **'Dilli Chalo', 'Give me blood...'**; **INA trials (Red Fort, 1945)**.

items: CDM = Dandi Salt March (1930); Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931; Quit India 1942 = 'Do or Die'.
INA under Bose; Red Fort INA trials (1945) galvanised opinion; RIN Mutiny (1946).

prelimsPointers: **Civil Disobedience** began with the **Dandi Salt March (12 March 1930)** from Sabarmati to Dandi.
**Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** → Gandhi attended the **2nd Round Table Conference**.
**Poona Pact (1932)** — Gandhi & Ambedkar; reserved seats (joint electorate) for Depressed Classes (after Communal Award).
**Quit India (8 Aug 1942, Bombay)** — slogan **'Do or Die'**; **August Kranti**.
Parallel governments — **Tamluk (Bengal), Satara (Maharashtra), Talcher**.
**INA (Azad Hind Fauj)** — reorganised by **Subhas Chandra Bose (1943)**; slogans **'Dilli Chalo', 'Jai Hind'**.
**INA/Red Fort Trials (1945)** and the **RIN (Naval) Mutiny (1946)** eroded British control.
mainsAngles: Assess the contribution of the Quit India Movement and the INA to India's independence.

glossary.definition: Gandhi's 1930 salt march that launched the Civil Disobedience Movement.
The 1942 'Do or Die' mass movement demanding an immediate end to British rule.
The Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj) led by Subhas Chandra Bose to liberate India by force.

sections.heading: Sardar Patel & Subhas Chandra Bose — roles

blocks.text: **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** (the 'Iron Man' / 'Bismarck of India') and **Subhas Chandra Bose** (Netaji) were two towering nationalists — Patel the **organiser and unifier who integrated 560+ princely states**, Bose the **radical who sought freedom through armed struggle and the INA**.

rows: Kheda & **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928 — earned 'Sardar')**; first **Home Minister & Deputy PM**; **integrated ~560 princely states** (with V.P. Menon); 'Iron Man of India'.
Twice **Congress President (Haripura 1938, Tripuri 1939 — resigned over Gandhi)**; founded **Forward Bloc (1939)**; led the **INA**; 'Netaji'; **'Give me blood, I will give you freedom'**.
Patel — organisation & unity within Congress; Bose — militant, international (Axis) route to freedom.

items: Patel = Bardoli (1928, 'Sardar') + integration of princely states + first Home Minister.
Bose = Congress President (Tripuri 1939) → Forward Bloc → INA (Netaji).

prelimsPointers: **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928)** earned Vallabhbhai Patel the title **'Sardar'**.
Patel — first **Home Minister & Deputy PM**; integrated **~560 princely states** (aided by V.P. Menon).
Patel — 'Iron Man of India'; **Statue of Unity** commemorates him.
**Subhas Chandra Bose** — Congress President at **Haripura (1938)** & **Tripuri (1939)**; resigned after differences with Gandhi.
Bose founded the **Forward Bloc (1939)** and led the **INA**; title **'Netaji'**.
Bose's slogans — **'Dilli Chalo', 'Jai Hind', 'Give me blood, I will give you freedom'**.
Bose set up the **Azad Hind (Provisional) Government** in Singapore (1943).
mainsAngles: Compare the contributions of Sardar Patel and Subhas Chandra Bose to the freedom struggle.

glossary.definition: The 1928 Gujarat no-tax peasant campaign led by Vallabhbhai Patel, earning him the title 'Sardar'.
The radical party founded by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1939 after leaving the Congress presidency.
Patel's post-1947 unification of ~560 princely states into the Indian Union.

blocks.text: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** — jurist, economist and social revolutionary — was the **chief architect of the Indian Constitution** as **Chairman of the Drafting Committee**, and the foremost champion of **Dalit rights and social justice**, whose life's mission was the annihilation of caste.

rows: **Mahad Satyagraha (1927), Kalaram Temple Entry (1930)**; burned the Manusmriti; journals **Mooknayak, Bahishkrit Bharat**.
Founded **Independent Labour Party, Scheduled Castes Federation**; **Poona Pact (1932)** with Gandhi.
**Chairman, Drafting Committee**; called the **'Father of the Indian Constitution'**; first **Law Minister**.
Resigned over the **Hindu Code Bill**; converted to **Buddhism (1956, Nagpur)**; **Bharat Ratna (1990)**.

items: Chairman of the Drafting Committee = 'Father of the Constitution'; first Law Minister.
Mahad Satyagraha (1927), Poona Pact (1932), Buddhist conversion (1956) — key life events.

prelimsPointers: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** — **Chairman of the Drafting Committee**; 'Father of the Indian Constitution'.
First **Law Minister** of independent India.
**Mahad Satyagraha (1927)** — for Dalit access to public water; burned the **Manusmriti**.
**Poona Pact (1932)** with Gandhi — reserved seats within a joint electorate for Depressed Classes.
Journals — **Mooknayak, Bahishkrit Bharat**; work **'Annihilation of Caste'**.
Converted to **Buddhism at Nagpur (1956)**; awarded **Bharat Ratna (posthumously, 1990)**.
Founded the **Reserve Bank of India blueprint** (via 'The Problem of the Rupee').
mainsAngles: Evaluate Ambedkar's role in Constitution-making and social justice.

glossary.definition: The Constituent Assembly committee chaired by Ambedkar that prepared the draft Constitution.
Ambedkar's 1927 campaign for Dalit rights to draw water from a public tank.
The 1932 Gandhi-Ambedkar agreement providing reserved seats for Depressed Classes within a joint electorate.

blocks.text: After independence, India was welded together by the **integration of ~560 princely states (Patel & V.P. Menon)** and then reorganised on **linguistic lines** — a process in which **Andhra led the way**, with **Potti Sriramulu's martyrdom** creating the first linguistic state (Andhra, 1953).

rows: **Patel & V.P. Menon** merged ~560 states via the **Instrument of Accession**; hard cases — **Junagadh, Hyderabad (Operation Polo, 1948), Kashmir**.
**Potti Sriramulu's fast unto death (Dec 1952)** → first **linguistic state, Andhra (1 Oct 1953)** from Madras.
**States Reorganisation Commission**; led to the **States Reorganisation Act (1956)** — 14 states & 6 UTs.
Andhra + Telangana (Hyderabad State) merged → **Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1956)**; bifurcated again in **2014 (Telangana)**.

items: Integration = Patel + V.P. Menon (Instrument of Accession); Hyderabad = Operation Polo (1948).
Potti Sriramulu → Andhra (1953, first linguistic state); Fazl Ali → SRA 1956 → AP (1956).

prelimsPointers: **Sardar Patel & V.P. Menon** integrated **~560 princely states** via the **Instrument of Accession**.
**Hyderabad** annexed by **Operation Polo (Sept 1948)**; **Junagadh** by plebiscite; Kashmir acceded (Oct 1947).
**Potti Sriramulu** died fasting (Dec 1952) demanding a Telugu state → **Andhra State (1 Oct 1953)** — India's **first linguistic state**.
**Dhar Commission & JVP Committee** initially opposed purely linguistic states.
**Fazl Ali Commission (SRC, 1953-55)** → **States Reorganisation Act (1956)**.
**Andhra Pradesh formed (1 Nov 1956)** by merging Andhra & Telangana (with the Gentlemen's Agreement).
AP was **bifurcated in 2014** creating **Telangana** (2 June 2014).
mainsAngles: Discuss the integration of princely states and the linguistic reorganisation of states, with reference to Andhra.

glossary.definition: The legal document by which princely states joined the Indian Union.
The 1948 police action integrating Hyderabad State into India.
The activist whose fast-unto-death led to the first linguistic state, Andhra (1953).

sections.heading: Constitutional acts & missions 1909–1947 (Morley-Minto to Cabinet Mission)

blocks.text: The **constitutional development of British India (1909–1947)** unfolded through a series of **Acts and missions** that gradually — and grudgingly — expanded Indian participation, from the **Morley-Minto reforms** to the **Cabinet Mission** that framed the path to independence.

rows: **Separate electorates for Muslims** (communal representation); expanded legislative councils.
**Dyarchy** in provinces; bicameral centre; **preamble on 'responsible government'**.
**Provincial autonomy**; abolished dyarchy in provinces; federal scheme (never fully implemented); Federal Court.
Rejected Pakistan; proposed a **grouping/federal plan** & the **Constituent Assembly**.

items: Morley-Minto 1909 = separate electorates; Mont-Ford 1919 = dyarchy; GoI 1935 = provincial autonomy.
Cripps ('post-dated cheque'); Cabinet Mission 1946 = Constituent Assembly; Mountbatten → Independence Act 1947.

prelimsPointers: **Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)** — introduced **separate electorates for Muslims**.
**Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms / GoI Act 1919** — **dyarchy** in the provinces; bicameral central legislature.
**Government of India Act 1935** — **provincial autonomy**; proposed an all-India **federation**; **RBI & Federal Court** set up.
**Cripps Mission (1942)** — Dominion status after WWII; rejected — Gandhi's **'post-dated cheque'**.
**Cabinet Mission (1946)** — rejected Pakistan; provided for the **Constituent Assembly** (grouping plan).
**Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)** → **Indian Independence Act 1947** → Partition.
The **1935 Act** was the longest and formed the basis of much of the Indian Constitution.
mainsAngles: Trace the constitutional developments from 1909 to 1947 leading to independence.

glossary.definition: The 1919 division of provincial subjects into 'reserved' and 'transferred', the latter under Indian ministers.
The 1946 British mission that rejected Pakistan and set up the framework for the Constituent Assembly.
The 1935 Act's grant of self-government to provinces under elected Indian ministries.
